title: fix(v4): enforce the six JSON Schema keywords fromJSONSchema silently dropped
body:
`fromJSONSchema` lists six validation keywords in `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` and silently drops them: `minProperties`, `maxProperties`, `uniqueItems`, `contains`, `minContains`, `maxContains`. A converted schema accepts data the source schema rejects, which is the worst failure mode for a validating converter — the file already throws for `not` and `if/then/else` rather than ignoring them.

```ts
const schema = z.fromJSONSchema({ type: "object", minProperties: 1 });
schema.safeParse({}).success; // main: true — now false
```

All six are now enforced inside the converter, with no new public API — nothing to undo when the @zod/json push happens. The property counts fold into the pre-pipe guard that already enforces `propertyNames`, so they see the raw input: a key synthesized by a property `default` does not satisfy `minProperties`, and a dropped `__proto__` still counts, matching how JSON Schema validators see the instance. `uniqueItems` and the `contains` family run as checks on the converted array schema, with structural equality (two objects with the same entries in different key order are duplicates). Each keyword is also carried into metadata the way `propertyNames` already is, so `toJSONSchema` round-trips all of them.

The `uniqueItems`/`contains` issues are `code: "custom"` with explicit messages, since no built-in issue code describes a match count; explicit messages bypass error maps, which seems acceptable for an experimental converter. `contentEncoding`/`contentMediaType`/`contentSchema` already flow into metadata on main and needed no change.

Three boundaries are deliberate rather than accidental. The keywords apply only under an explicit single `type`, matching how the converter already treats a typeless `minLength` or `minimum`; and on a union `type` like `["array", "null"]` they are enforced but not carried into metadata, the same round-trip gap `propertyNames` has today. And because the guard sits on the input side of a pipe, a guard issue aborts before `minItems`/`maxItems` are reported, and `toJSONSchema` strips `default`/`examples` from the `io: "input"` document — the price of evaluating the keywords against the raw instance, which the `propertyNames` guard has paid since it shipped. All of these, plus re-emitting a carried `contains` that points into `$defs`, belong to the converter's existing contract and the future @zod/json work; each is pinned by a test so it reads as a decision.

The two cardinality issues carry an explicit English `message`. `origin: "object"` has no `Sizable` entry in any locale, so the structured pipeline renders "expected object to be >=2" — a value comparison rather than a count, wrong in all 62 locales. An accurate message in one language beats a misleading one in every language; giving the locales an `object` entry is the fix, and it belongs with the first-class checks rather than here.

## Three axes

Measured against the merge-base with esbuild `--minify` and `gzip -9 -n` under `--conditions=@zod/source`:

| axis | result |
| --- | --- |
| bundle, classic importing `fromJSONSchema` | 36,736 → 37,567 B gz (+831; raw +2,878) |
| bundle, classic `z.object()` and `zod/mini` | +0 B — neither reaches the converter |
| construction, guarded object | 12.6 → 20.9 µs, once per schema |
| parse, guarded object | 0.03 → 0.07 µs |
| parse, 10-element array | 0.30 µs plain, 1.39 µs `uniqueItems`, 0.71 µs `contains` |
| retained per schema | 6.8 KB plain, 10.9 KB with the object guard, 9.9 KB with the array guard |

The whole cost is opt-in twice over: only a document that writes one of these keywords builds a guard, and only a bundle that imports `fromJSONSchema` carries the code. Machine load was elevated throughout, so the timings are ratios rather than absolutes; they held across two runs, and the memory figures were byte-identical.

Everything lands in `from-json-schema.ts`, so mini pays nothing and classic bundles that never import `fromJSONSchema` are byte-identical; the cost lands only on its users.

Closes #6463

> [!IMPORTANT] > The four array keywords validate the parsed output instead of the raw instance, which lets `contains` accept an array the source schema rejects. **Reviewed changes** — the full diff of commit `30468ab`, which attaches enforcement to the six keywords `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` was consuming without effect. - **`checkPropertyNames` → `checkObjectGuards`** — the existing pre-pipe key guard now also enforces `minProperties`/`maxProperties`, pushing `too_small`/`too_big` with `origin: "object"`. Running ahead of the object parse is deliberate so the counts see the raw instance. - **`uniqueItems`** — a new `jsonDeepEqual` helper backs a post-parse check that reports each duplicate index against the first element it matches. - **`contains`/`minContains`/`maxContains`** — a post-parse check counts matching items and pushes `code: "custom"` issues with explicit messages; `minContains` defaults to 1, `maxContains` is unbounded when absent. - **Metadata carry** — all six are stashed into `extraMeta` the way `propertyNames` already was, gated on a single-string `type` and no `$ref`, so `toJSONSchema` re-emits them. - **Tests** — four cases covering property counts against raw input, composition with `propertyNames`, structural duplicates, and the `contains` bounds including `minContains: 0`. I confirmed the new checks cannot crash on a non-array input — `runChecks` skips checks once the payload has aborted, and `invalid_type` aborts — and that tuples built from `prefixItems` or a draft-7 `items` array are covered. `jsonDeepEqual` matches the spec's instance-equality definition. The full `from-json-schema` and `to-json-schema` suites pass in both the normal and compile-mode projects. One thing I looked at and decided against raising as a finding: `contains` postdates draft-4 and `minContains`/`maxContains` postdate draft-7, so a strict reading says they should be inert in those dialects. The converter doesn't gate anything else that way either — a draft-4 document with `prefixItems` still builds a tuple — and ignoring a keyword the author explicitly wrote is the bug this PR is fixing. Leaving it ungated looks right. ### ℹ️ The keywords are still dropped when `type` isn't a single string Enforcement only happens inside `convertBaseSchema`'s `object` and `array` cases, so `{ "minProperties": 1 }` with no `type` still converts to `z.any()` and accepts everything — the same silent drop the PR is closing, just one level up. This matches how typeless `minLength`, `minimum` and `pattern` already behave in this converter, so it may well be out of scope, but the PR's framing invites the question. Worth deciding explicitly rather than by omission, since `{"minProperties": 1}` as a bare `allOf`/`anyOf` branch is a common idiom for "at least one key". A smaller sibling: with `type: ["array", "null"]` the guards *do* apply, because each member is re-entered through `convertBaseSchema`, but the metadata carry is skipped since it tests `schema.type === "array"`. So those schemas validate correctly and then round-trip lossily.

The pre-existing `propertyNames` carry has the identical union-typed blind spot, so fixing it here would be a separate, broader change. ````

inline.body:
These two checks are appended to the converted array schema, so they run *after* the parse and see the parsed output rather than the instance — the exact hazard `checkObjectGuards` goes out of its way to avoid twenty lines up. A `default` on a property inside `items` is enough to break both directions, and the `contains` direction is a false accept.

```ts
const items = { type: "object", properties: { a: { type: "string", default: "x" } } };

// accepts [{}] — the default synthesizes the match. JSON Schema rejects: no item has `a`.
z.fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", items, contains: { type: "object", properties: { a: { const: "x" } }, required: ["a"] } })
  .safeParse([{}]).success; // true

// rejects [{a:"x"}, {}] — both become {a:"x"}. JSON Schema accepts: two distinct items.
z.fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", items, uniqueItems: true })
  .safeParse([{ a: "x" }, {}]).success; // false
```

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# `uniqueItems` and `contains` validate the parsed output, not the instance

## Affected sites
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:636-653` — the `uniqueItems` check reads `payload.value` after the array/tuple parse has applied defaults, so two items that differed in the instance can compare equal. False reject.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:656-683` — the `contains` check counts matches over the same post-parse value, so an item that did not satisfy `contains` in the instance can satisfy it after a default fills in the deciding property. False accept, which the PR description itself calls the worst failure mode for a validating converter.

## Required outcome
Both keywords must be evaluated against the array as it was received, matching the raw-input rule the object guard already documents and the property-count tests already assert. Nested `default`s are the reachable trigger today; anything else that makes the parsed array differ from the instance has the same effect.

## Suggested approach
The machinery is already in the file. `checkObjectGuards` wraps its subject as `z.transform(identity).check(...).pipe(objectSchema)` precisely so the check observes raw input; an array-side equivalent would do the same, with the `Array.isArray` early return standing in for the object type test. That also keeps both halves of the PR explaining themselves the same way instead of two mechanisms with opposite semantics.

Worth a regression test with a `default` nested in `items` for each keyword — the four new tests all use item schemas that parse to themselves, so they pass either way.
````

</details>

`origin: "object"` has no entry in the locales' `Sizable` map, so these fall to the non-sizable branch and render as a value comparison rather than a count: `"Too small: expected object to be >=2"` and `"Too big: expected object to be <=3"`. Compare the array equivalent, `"Too small: expected array to have >=2 items"`.

An explicit `message` on the two issues would fix it without touching the forty-odd locale files, and would be consistent with the explicit messages you already accepted for `uniqueItems`/`contains` in this PR.

Addressed in `0ea26fad` — both keywords now run pre-pipe via `checkArrayGuards`, with a regression test using a `default` nested in `items`.   ｜ [View workflow run](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/actions/runs/33430102659/job/99613120043) ｜ via [Pullfrog](https://pullfrog.com) ｜ Using `Claude Opus` ｜ [𝕏](https://x.com/pullfrogai)

Addressed in `0ea26fad` — both issues now carry an explicit `message` naming the property count.   ｜ [View workflow run](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/actions/runs/33430102659/job/99613120043) ｜ via [Pullfrog](https://pullfrog.com) ｜ Using `Claude Opus` ｜ [𝕏](https://x.com/pullfrogai)

Now that the guard sits on the input side of the pipe, a guard issue aborts before the array parses — so `minItems`/`maxItems` are no longer reported when a guard keyword also fails. Verified on `{type:"array", items:{type:"integer"}, minItems:3, uniqueItems:true}` with `[1,1]`: only the `custom` duplicate issue, no `too_small`. Under the old placement both surfaced, since `too_small` carries `continue: true`.

Rejection is unchanged, so this is diagnostics only — but it's the one case where the move is a strict loss rather than a swap, and nothing tests it.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# `minItems`/`maxItems` issues are swallowed when a guard keyword fails

## Affected sites
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:705-713` — the guard wraps the array schema, and `handlePipeResult` (`core/schemas.ts:4340`) aborts the pipe on any issue other than `unrecognized_keys`, so the right side never runs.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:691-696`, `:664-669`, `:679-684` — `minItems`/`maxItems` land on the array/tuple schema, i.e. on the suppressed side.

## Verified
- New: `{type:"array",items:{type:"integer"},minItems:3,uniqueItems:true}` on `[1,1]` → `[{code:"custom",path:[1]}]`.
- Old placement, simulated as `z.array(z.int()).min(3).check(guard)` on `[1,1]` → `[{code:"too_small"},{code:"custom",path:[1]}]`.
- Same for `maxItems`, and for the `prefixItems` tuple branch.
- Element type errors flip the same way, but that direction is a swap: the old placement reported them and skipped the guard, so neither placement ever showed both.

## Required outcome
Either the length keywords co-report with the guard keywords again, or the precedence is accepted deliberately and pinned by a test so it doesn't read as an oversight.

## Suggested approach
Folding `minItems`/`maxItems` into `checkArrayGuards` would restore co-reporting — array length is identical before and after the item parse, so they're safe to evaluate on the raw instance. That does mean the length keywords take two different code paths depending on whether a guard keyword is present, which may not be worth it for a diagnostics-only difference; accepting and testing it is a reasonable answer too.
````

</details>

The identity transform makes `isTransforming()` true for the whole schema, and `toJSONSchema` deletes `default` and `examples` from a transforming schema in `io: "input"` mode. So adding any guard keyword silently strips them from the input-mode document:

```ts
z.toJSONSchema(z.fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", uniqueItems: true, default: [] }), { io: "input" });
// { type: "array", items: {}, uniqueItems: true }   — no `default`
// drop `uniqueItems` from the source and `default` comes back
```

This is a regression against `main` for `{type:"object", minProperties:1, default:{}}` too, which previously built no guard at all. Default (`io: "output"`) mode is unaffected.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# A guard keyword strips `default`/`examples` from the `io: "input"` document

## Affected sites
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:293` — `return guard.pipe(arraySchema)` puts a `$ZodTransform` on the pipe's `in` side.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:632-645` — same wrapper is now reached for `minProperties`/`maxProperties` alone, which on `main` produced a bare `ZodObject`.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/core/to-json-schema.ts:276-280` — deletes `result.schema.default` and `.examples` when `isTransforming(schema)`; `isTransforming` follows a pipe to its transform `in`.

## Verified
- `{type:"array", uniqueItems:true, default:[], examples:[[1]]}` → `io:"input"` emits neither `default` nor `examples`; the same document without `uniqueItems` emits both.
- `{type:"object", minProperties:1, default:{}, examples:[{a:1}]}` → identical loss, and identical to what `propertyNames` already did on `main`.
- Nested under a parent object, `properties.xs.default` is dropped in input mode and present in output mode.
- `io: "output"` is correct in every case; `pipeProcessor` resolves to `def.out` when `def.in` is a transform.

## Required outcome
A converted schema should emit the same annotations in input mode whether or not one of the six keywords is present. Failing that, the limitation should be a deliberate, recorded boundary like the other two in the PR description.

## Open questions for the human
- Is `io: "input"` fidelity in scope here, or does it belong with the `@zod/json` work alongside the `contains`/`$defs` gap? The `propertyNames` guard has had this since it shipped, so this PR widens the blast radius rather than creating the mechanism — but `minProperties` on a plain object is a much more ordinary document than `propertyNames`.
- If it is in scope: re-applying `default`/`examples` onto the wrapper after `checkObjectGuards`/`checkArrayGuards` is the narrow fix; teaching `isTransforming` to see through an identity transform is the general one and is a `core/` change with its own three-axis cost.
````

</details>

These standard `too_small`/`too_big` issues hard-code English, so per-parse, global, and locale error maps can never customize them because `finalizeIssue` takes `issue.message` first. Drop the explicit `message` on both object-cardinality issues so the normal structured-issue pipeline formats them.

Counting in full makes `contains` reparse every raw item even after the result is decided: without `maxContains`, reaching `minContains` proves success, while exceeding `maxContains` proves failure. Short-circuit those cases instead of paying for exact-count prose, which can nearly double validation work for large or expensive item schemas.

Copying the raw `contains` schema into metadata does not copy the root `$defs`, so a valid source with `contains: { $ref: "#/$defs/Hit" }` emits an unresolved reference and Ajv rejects the output. The emitted document must retain or rewrite referenced definitions, or avoid advertising a `contains` value it cannot make self-contained.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# Preserve definitions referenced by `contains`

## Affected sites
- packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:841-842 — raw source metadata is copied without its definition graph
- packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/from-json-schema.test.ts — the round-trip tests only cover an inline `contains`

## Required outcome
- Every `$ref` emitted from carried `contains` metadata resolves in the generated document.
- Add a regression case with root `$defs` and compile the emitted schema with Ajv, rather than asserting output shape alone.
````

</details>

`containsRef` descends into every object value, including instance-valued annotations, so `default: { $ref: "literal" }` is mistaken for a schema reference. That drops an otherwise valid `contains` or `propertyNames` constraint from the round-trip and broadens the emitted schema.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# Reference-shaped annotation data drops constraints

## Affected sites
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:260` — the unrestricted `Object.values()` recursion treats `$ref` inside `default`, `const`, `enum`, or `examples` data as a schema keyword
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:840-849` — the false positive suppresses the entire carried `propertyNames` or `contains` subschema

## Required outcome
- Omit metadata only for actual schema references that would become unresolved, without interpreting `$ref` properties inside instance-valued annotations as references.
- Add a regression case such as `{ type: "array", contains: { type: "integer", default: { $ref: "literal" } } }`; the source and converted schema reject `["x"]`, and the round-tripped schema must reject it too.

## Suggested approach
Walk only schema-valued keyword positions, or explicitly exclude instance-valued annotation keywords before recursing.
````

</details>

`dependencies` is a schema map in draft-7 and draft-4, but it is absent from this allowlist. A carried subschema with `dependencies: { a: { $ref: "#/definitions/Hit" } }` now passes `containsRef`, and `toJSONSchema` emits that `$ref` without the root `definitions`, leaving an invalid output document.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# Walk schema-valued `dependencies` entries

## Affected sites
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:277` — `SCHEMA_MAP_KEYWORDS` omits draft-7/draft-4 `dependencies`, whose map values may be either property-name arrays or schemas.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts:886` — the resulting false negative carries `contains` verbatim after its root definitions have been discarded.

## Required outcome
- Detect `$ref` inside schema-valued `dependencies` entries without treating array-valued property dependencies as schemas.
- Add a draft-7 regression where the dependency schema references root `definitions` and confirm the dangling `contains` metadata is not emitted.

## Suggested approach
- Handle `dependencies` separately from the all-schema maps, recursing only into non-array values.
````

</details>
